w1.bigIdea: Computers strictly execute literal instructions without human intuition or context. Algorithms must be completely unambiguous.
w1.setupPrep: Set up a clean demonstration table at the front of the circle rug. Unpack bread, a jar of jam with the lid tightly closed, a butter knife, and plates. Prepare paper clipboards for Upper Elementary coders.
w1.title: The Great Story & The Jam Sandwich Robot
w1.montessori: Practical Life (Grace & Courtesy, Sequence of Work)
w1.primaryDesc: 1-step physical actions; physically perform step before giving command to Teacher Robot.
w1.elementaryDesc: Pair work writing precise written algorithm on paper prior to live testing on Teacher Robot.
steps: Gather students on the circle rug and tell the Great Story of how humans communicate with computers.
Introduce the 'Teacher Robot' who only understands literal, step-by-step commands.
Place bread, butter, and jam on the table. Ask Primary students to give one physical command at a time.
Have Upper El students write down a 5-step sandwich algorithm before testing it on the robot.
Observe as the Robot follows instructions literally (e.g., placing unopened jam jar on top of bread if 'put jam on bread' is commanded).
w1.controlOfError: Literal execution by the Teacher Robot. If an instruction is missing 'open the lid', the robot attempts to spread the sealed jar, making the bug immediately obvious without teacher correction.

w2.bigIdea: Algorithms guide spatial movement step-by-step. Directional instructions require precise orientation and unambiguous relative steps.
w2.setupPrep: Tape a 3x3 (Primary) and 5x5 (Elementary) grid on the floor using painter's masking tape. Place target objects (plush toy or beanbag) in destination squares. Lay out directional cards.
keyMaterials: Arrow cards (Forward, Turn Left, Turn Right)
w2.title: Kidbots Part 1: The Floor Grid & Arrows
w2.primaryDesc: 3x3 Floor Grid. Concrete action: place physical arrow cards directly on grid squares ahead of Robot child.
w2.elementaryDesc: 5x5 Floor Grid. Abstract action: programmer lays out full arrow card sequence on external mat before Robot moves.
steps: Set up a masking-tape floor grid (3x3 for Primary, 5x5 for Elementary) and place a target object in one cell.
Designate one student as the 'Robot' and another as the 'Programmer'.
For Primary: The Programmer walks alongside the Robot, placing physical Arrow Cards (Forward, Turn Left, Turn Right) square by square.
For Elementary: The Programmer creates a sequence on an external Command Mat before sending the Robot on its path.
Review precision: Ensure turns (90 degrees) happen in-place without moving forward.
w2.controlOfError: The physical grid lines. If the Robot steps off the grid or lands in a blank cell away from the target, the Programmer can re-trace their arrow sequence.

w3.bigIdea: Errors ('bugs') are natural in programming; debugging is the systematic process of identifying, isolating, and correcting flawed steps.
w3.setupPrep: Maintain floor grids from W2. Place 1 cone on the 3x3 grid and 3 cones on the 5x5 grid. Prepare intentional buggy algorithm cards to test student debugging skills.
keyMaterials: Traffic cones or red felt obstacle pads
w3.title: Kidbots Part 2: Obstacles & Debugging
w3.primaryDesc: 3x3 Grid with 1 obstacle cone. Physically swap out single incorrect arrow card when robot hits obstacle.
w3.elementaryDesc: 5x5 Grid with 3 obstacles. Identify bugs in peer sequences and compare two valid paths to determine efficiency.
steps: Introduce obstacle cones or red felt pads on the grid map.
Intentionally present a faulty arrow card sequence that leads the Robot straight into an obstacle.
Guide students to 'pause' the robot at the exact step where the error occurs.
Have students isolate the bad card, replace it with the correct directional card, and resume execution.
Challenge Upper El students to find the shortest possible algorithm (fewest total steps).
w3.controlOfError: Physical obstacle cones. Collision with a cone halts the Robot immediately, indicating an error in the current card position.

w4.bigIdea: Repetition can be compressed using loops and reusable subroutines, making code dramatically more efficient and easier to maintain.
w4.setupPrep: Lay out an extended linear grid track on the rug with repeating path sections. Place 'Rescue Target' at the end. Prepare 'Repeat (N)' loop cards and Function mats.
w4.title: Rescue Mission: Loops, Functions & Algorithmic Efficiency
w4.primaryDesc: Physical rhythm: clap or stomp for repeated actions ('Step, Clap, Step, Clap' -> 'Repeat 2 times').
w4.elementaryDesc: Re-write 10-step Kidbot path using Repeat Commands and Subroutines/Function Blocks to condense code under 5 total blocks.
steps: Set up a longer grid course with repeating path patterns (e.g., 3 forward steps, or repeating stair patterns).
Introduce the Repeat Loop card and Function definition mats.
Demonstrate how 3 'Forward' cards can be represented by a single '3x Forward' loop block.
Have Elementary students write a Function block on a dry-erase card, then call that function name inside their main algorithm.
Run the Robot child through the compressed program.
w4.controlOfError: Step counting. If a loop executes 3 times instead of 2, the Robot overshoots the target square on the grid.

w5.bigIdea: Conditional logic allows programs to make decisions and adapt execution based on dynamic inputs and environmental states.
w5.setupPrep: Place colored felt squares (Red, Blue) at grid decision junctions. Set up IF/THEN/ELSE command cards on stands for programmer reference.
w5.title: Conditional Logic & Decision Paths
w5.primaryDesc: Concrete physical rules: 'IF stepping on red mat, THEN turn right, ELSE walk straight forward.'
w5.elementaryDesc: Construct floor grid branching paths using IF/THEN/ELSE condition cards and test edge-case choices.
steps: Lay out colored felt squares (Red/Blue) on specific intersection points of the floor grid.
Introduce 'IF/THEN' logic cards: 'IF on Red square THEN turn Left ELSE turn Right'.
Send the Robot down the path, requiring them to inspect the floor color before choosing their next step.
Have Elementary students design branching paths for peer programmers to solve.
Discuss real-world conditionals (e.g., 'IF it rains THEN grab an umbrella').
w5.controlOfError: Color-coded path mismatch. Stepping off the intended path indicates a failure to evaluate the IF/THEN condition correctly.

w6.bigIdea: All digital data is built from binary states (ON/OFF, 1/0). Exponential base-2 place values (1, 2, 4, 8, 16) allow representing any integer.
w6.setupPrep: Print or construct oversized binary dot cards (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 dots). Arrange student pairs on the rug with individual card sets.
w6.title: Binary Numbers Part 1: Dots, Switches & Base-2
w6.primaryDesc: 3 Binary Dot Cards (4, 2, 1); practice counting dots and flipping cards ON (visible) and OFF (blank).
w6.elementaryDesc: 5 Binary Dot Cards (16, 8, 4, 2, 1); practice place values and count sequentially from 0 to 31 in binary systems.
steps: Demonstrate binary cards with dots (1, 2, 4, 8, 16) arranged in order from right to left.
Explain the rule: Cards are either face-up (1/ON) or face-down (0/OFF).
Ask students to flip cards to show specific numbers by adding dot values together.
Demonstrate binary counting sequences starting from 0 (all down) up to the maximum value.
Have Upper El write down numbers in binary notation (e.g., 5 = 101).
w6.controlOfError: Visual dot count verification. Adding up the visible dots confirms whether the correct decimal target number was achieved.

w7.bigIdea: Letters and text are represented in computers by mapping binary numbers to character codes (e.g., 5-bit ASCII-style alphabet codes).
w7.setupPrep: Pre-cut string or pipe cleaners. Organize pony beads into two distinct high-contrast colors (e.g., Black=0, White=1). Distribute 5-bit alphabet charts.
w7.title: Binary Numbers Part 2: Binary Alphabet & Counting
w7.montessori: Language Work & History of Writing (4th Great Lesson)
w7.primaryDesc: Encode first initial using 5 physical black/white tiles or bead sequences.
w7.elementaryDesc: Encode 4-letter secret word into 5-Bit ASCII binary encoding; craft bead bracelets and decode peer messages.
steps: Introduce the 5-bit binary alphabet chart linking numbers 1–26 to letters A–Z.
Provide two colors of beads (e.g., black for 0, white for 1) and stringing wire.
Guide students to look up their initial/name letters and decode them into 5-bit binary sequences.
Thread beads sequentially onto wire to create a binary wristband or bookmark.
Have students swap crafts with a partner to decode each other's hidden messages.
w7.controlOfError: Alphabet chart lookup verification. Decoding a partner's bead pattern yields their actual name or secret word.

w8.bigIdea: Digital images are composed of a grid matrix of tiny pixels, where binary numbers dictate shading and color codes for each pixel cell.
w8.setupPrep: Print 5x5 (Primary) and 10x10 (Elementary) pixel grid worksheets. Prepare colored pencils or markers matching the palette key.
w8.title: Image Representation: Pixels, Grids & Color by Numbers
w8.primaryDesc: 3-color palette (0=White, 1=Red, 2=Yellow) 5x5 grid. Copy visual card showing a simple pixel heart directly onto grid.
w8.elementaryDesc: 5-color palette on 10x10 grid. Decode raw binary code strings line-by-line into bitmaps to reveal hidden pixel art image.
steps: Display a large grid image and explain that digital screens are made up of tiny picture elements called pixels.
Hand out blank pixel grid sheets and binary pixel maps.
Explain the rule: 0 = white/light, 1 = black/dark.
Have students fill in grid cells row by row according to the binary string.
Introduce color pixel art for Elementary students using numbers (e.g., 1 = Red, 2 = Blue).
w8.controlOfError: Recognizable picture outcome. Correct pixel shading reveals a distinct image (e.g., heart, star, or smiley face).

w9.bigIdea: Data compression reduces file size by storing counts of repeated consecutive values rather than recording every individual bit.
w9.setupPrep: Prepare side-by-side comparison posters showing uncompressed binary vs. RLE compressed strings (e.g., 4W, 3B, 3W). Print RLE grid worksheets.
w9.title: Data Compression: Run-Length Encoding
w9.primaryDesc: Physical bead compression: group 5 identical white beads and place number tag '5' next to single bead.
w9.elementaryDesc: 10x10 grid challenge using RLE code strings (e.g., 2W, 4B, 2W); squeeze pixel codes and calculate percentage saved.
steps: Compare a full uncompressed binary string (0000111000) with its run-length equivalent (4W, 3B, 3W).
Explain that Run-Length Encoding (RLE) saves storage by counting repeating data runs.
Provide RLE code sheets for students to decode onto blank grid paper.
Have Upper El write their own RLE codes for custom pixel drawings.
Calculate the compression ratio: count total characters before vs. after compression.
w9.controlOfError: Grid length matching. A correctly decoded RLE line fills the grid row without overflowing or leaving empty cells.

w10.bigIdea: Text compression replaces repetitive words and patterns with short dictionary keys or pointers, drastically reducing storage footprint.
w10.setupPrep: Print nursery rhymes or short stories formatted with high phrase repetition. Prepare symbol/dictionary cards and highlighters.
w10.title: Text & Pattern Compression
w10.primaryDesc: Symbol replacement: substitute recurring story words with physical picture tokens.
w10.elementaryDesc: Compress nursery rhymes using dictionary keys, pointers, and redundancy reduction cards.
steps: Sing a familiar song or poem with repeated refrains (e.g., 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star').
Identify repeating words or phrases and assign them a symbol/dictionary card.
Replace all occurrences of those phrases in the poem with their symbol cards.
Have Elementary students build a custom dictionary key for short paragraphs.
Compare the original character count to the compressed dictionary version.
w10.controlOfError: Reconstruction check. Replacing symbols back with dictionary phrases accurately reads as the complete original text.

w11.bigIdea: Computers use parity bits (even/odd calculations across matrix rows and columns) to detect when data has been corrupted during transmission.
w11.setupPrep: Prepare sets of two-sided magnetic or felt cards (Black on one side, White on the other). Arrange 3x3 or 5x5 grid spaces on magnetic boards or tables.
w11.title: Parity Magic Part 1: Error Detection
w11.primaryDesc: 3x3 card grid. Practice counting even/odd pairs of colored cards with teacher guidance.
w11.elementaryDesc: 5x5 card grid. Set up parity checksum row/column using even/odd grid matrix logic to perform 'magic trick' error detection.
steps: Lay out a grid of black-and-white cards (e.g., 4x4 or 5x5).
Add an extra row and column ('parity bits') so that every row and column has an EVEN number of black cards.
Have the demonstrator turn their back while a student flips exactly ONE card.
Scan row by row and column by column to spot the single row and column with an ODD number of black cards.
Point to the flipped card at the intersection of the odd row and column!
w11.controlOfError: Parity count contradiction. The flipped card is guaranteed to be at the exact intersection of the row and column with odd counts.

w12.activityName: Parity Magic Part 2: Checksums & Data Reliability
w12.bigIdea: Checksums and error-correcting codes allow networks to not only detect corrupted data, but automatically pinpoint and fix errors.
w12.setupPrep: Set up two 'Network Node' tables separated across the room. Prepare 'Transmission Packet' worksheets with row/column parity counts.
w12.title: Parity Magic Part 2: Checksums & Data Reliability
w12.primaryDesc: Identify altered card location in a 3x3 guided layout matrix.
w12.elementaryDesc: Complete 5x5 self-healing error correction matrix and simulate transmission verification across data networks.
steps: Explain how computers send data across network cables and need to confirm no bits got corrupted.
Demonstrate simple checksum calculation: adding numbers in a row and appending the total digit to the end.
Simulate corrupted transmission by changing one digit in a simulated data packet.
Have students compute the checksum on the receiving end to verify if the data was corrupted.
Explore real-world check digits on barcodes or product ISBNs.
w12.controlOfError: Checksum discrepancy. If computed checksum != received check digit, data corruption occurred.

w13.bigIdea: Searching sorted data using Binary Search (O(log N)) repeatedly halves the search space, making it exponentially faster than Linear Search (O(N)).
w13.setupPrep: Line up 10 (Primary) or 30 (Elementary) numbered plastic cups/cards in numerical order across a long table. Hide a small token under one item.
w13.title: Linear vs. Binary Search & Algorithmic Thinking
w13.primaryDesc: Cup search across 10 cups using physical flips and higher/lower visual prompts.
w13.elementaryDesc: Compare linear cup search vs. binary search across 30+ cups, recording total steps and proving O(log N) efficiency.
steps: Arrange numbered cards/cups in sequential order.
Demonstrate Linear Search: check items one by one from left to right until target is found.
Demonstrate Binary Search: reveal the middle item. If target is larger/smaller, discard half of remaining set!
Time and count the steps required for both methods.
Discuss why Binary Search requires far fewer steps on large ordered datasets.
w13.controlOfError: Target card/object location. Binary Search always isolates the target within ceil(log2 N) steps.

w14.bigIdea: Decision trees break complex classification problems into a hierarchy of binary YES/NO choices, optimizing search and AI decision-making.
w14.setupPrep: Prepare sets of 8 (Primary) or 16-20 (Elementary) animal/object cards. Draw a sample decision tree structure on the whiteboard.
w14.title: 20 Questions Algorithmic Search & Decision Trees
w14.primaryDesc: Search using 8 visual object cards with pre-drawn visual classification paths.
w14.elementaryDesc: Construct binary decision trees for 16–20 items on graph paper, tracing paths with minimal binary questions.
steps: Play 20 Questions to guess a target animal/object.
Highlight questions that eliminate half the options (e.g., 'Is it a living thing?') versus specific guesses.
Guide students to build a decision tree diagram branching into YES/NO paths on paper.
Test decision trees by tracing paths to classify new mystery objects.
Refine questions to minimize tree depth.
w14.controlOfError: Path tracing leading directly to the single target object at the terminal leaf node.

w15.bigIdea: Sorting networks process multiple data comparisons simultaneously (in parallel), achieving faster sorting than step-by-step sequential methods.
w15.setupPrep: Draw the classic 6-input CS Unplugged Sorting Network on outdoor pavement with sidewalk chalk or tape. Prepare large number cards (1-6).
w15.title: Sorting Networks Part 1: Outdoor Parallel Processing
w15.concept: Floor Grid Spatial Rules & Parallel Processing
w15.primaryDesc: 1-digit number cards; navigate outdoor chalk network following node spatial rules.
w15.elementaryDesc: Large 2-digit or 3-digit cards; time parallel network sorting with stopwatch to measure algorithm throughput speed.
steps: Draw a CS Unplugged 6-person Sorting Network on the floor using chalk or tape.
Assign 6 students random number cards and have them stand in the starting circles.
Students advance simultaneously along lines until they meet at a comparison node.
At each node, the lower number exits to the left, higher to the right.
Repeat until all students reach the destination circles sorted in perfect order!
w15.controlOfError: Destination circle values. Cards are automatically arranged in sorted order (1 to 6) at exit circles.

w16.activityName: Sorting Networks: Parallel vs. Serial Optimization
w16.bigIdea: Parallel algorithms leverage multiple concurrent pathways to drastically reduce execution clock time compared to serial single-processor sorting.
w16.setupPrep: Set up outdoor sorting network along with a parallel single-lane Bubble Sort station. Assign student timekeepers with stopwatches.
w16.title: Sorting Networks Part 2: Network Optimization & Timing
w16.primaryDesc: Sort physical objects by size (small, medium, large foam blocks) through outdoor chalk paths.
w16.elementaryDesc: Compare Parallel vs. Serial Sorting; reverse sort numbers descending and design custom 4-person network logic.
steps: Time a single student sorting 6 numbers sequentially using Bubble Sort.
Time 6 students running through the parallel Sorting Network simultaneously.
Compare total elapsed clock time between parallel vs. serial execution.
Discuss how multi-core computer processors run tasks in parallel to speed up computation.
Try reverse sorting (largest to smallest) by flipping node comparison rules.
w16.controlOfError: Stopwatch comparison data showing significantly fewer parallel execution cycles.

w17.activityName: Cryptography: Caesar Cipher Wheels & Key Shifts
w17.bigIdea: Encryption protects sensitive data by transforming plain text into ciphertext using mathematical key shifts and secret ciphers.
w17.setupPrep: Pre-cut inner and outer wheel templates on cardstock. Supply brass paper fasteners (split pins). Prepare secret message strips.
w17.title: Cryptography & Secret Codes Part 1: Ciphers & Secret Sharing
w17.montessori: History of Language & Secret Writing (4th Lesson)
w17.primaryDesc: Symbol substitution cipher matching physical picture symbols to decode secret words.
w17.elementaryDesc: Numerical Caesar Cipher wheels (+3 key shift); build secret sharing schemes and trade encrypted secret messages.
steps: Assemble paper Caesar Cipher wheels with brass fasteners.
Set inner and outer alphabet rings shifted by a secret key number (e.g., +3 shift).
Demonstrate encoding a message (A -> D) and decoding by reversing key shift.
Have students exchange encrypted notes and decode them using shared secret keys.
Discuss cybersecurity and private messaging over open networks.
w17.controlOfError: Decoded message output yields legible English words.

w18.bigIdea: Modulo arithmetic (remainder math) provides the mathematical foundation for modern wrap-around ciphers and public-key cryptography.
w18.setupPrep: Distribute 12-hour and 26-point circular clock dials. Draw modulo equation examples (15 mod 12 = 3) on the whiteboard.
w18.title: Cryptography Part 2: Modulo Math & Clock Arithmetic
w18.primaryDesc: Clock face math: practice 12-hour wrap-around arithmetic using movable clock hands.
w18.elementaryDesc: Remainder operations (A mod B) using 26-hour alphabet clock arithmetic to compute advanced wrap ciphers.
steps: Introduce Modulo arithmetic as 'remainder math' using a 12-hour clock dial.
Demonstrate how 10 + 5 = 15 = 3 mod 12.
Extend clock arithmetic to 26 letters in the alphabet using Modulo 26 math.
Show how key shifts wrapping past 'Z' wrap back around to 'A' using mod operations.
Practice modular arithmetic cipher problems on paper.
w18.controlOfError: Clock dial visual positions. Tracing around the dial matches computed modular remainders.

w19.bigIdea: Software engineering begins with conceptual design, storyboarding user interfaces, and mapping system logic via flowcharts before writing code.
w19.setupPrep: Prepare 3-panel storyboard templates and flowchart symbol legend cards (Start/End, Action, Decision, Input/Output).
w19.title: Applied Capstone Planning & Digital Mapping
w19.primaryDesc: Draw ScratchJr scene storyboards and assign motion/tap trigger arrows to recycling items.
w19.elementaryDesc: Storyboard capstone software projects (Garden Tracker / Eco-Sorter) using flowcharts and pseudocode mapping.
steps: Introduce the Capstone goal: convert unplugged logic into digital projects.
Brainstorm digital project ideas connected to CS Unplugged concepts (e.g., digital maze, binary quiz).
Draw storyboard frames depicting starting screen, main action, and game over/win screens.
Construct flowchart diagrams detailing user interactions and key events.
Review plans in peer feedback circles.
w19.controlOfError: Flowchart path completeness. Every decision box must have valid 'Yes' and 'No' exit paths.

w20.activityName: Applied Capstone Phase 1: Digital Interface Setup
w20.bigIdea: Digital applications require structuring graphical user interface (GUI) assets, spatial coordinates, and event listener triggers.
w20.setupPrep: Set up tablet/computer workstations with Scratch / ScratchJr loaded. Ensure project save folders are created for every student pair.
w20.title: Applied Capstone Phase 1: Digital Interface Setup
w20.primaryDesc: Program tap triggers and message envelopes in ScratchJr to play success sounds when items enter correct bins.
w20.elementaryDesc: Design custom plant/trash sprites and set up canvas interface with event triggers in Scratch.
steps: Set up student software workspaces or physical staging environments.
Design custom main character (sprite) and backdrop graphics.
Add basic trigger events (e.g., 'When Green Flag Clicked', 'When Space Key Pressed').
Program initial sprite placement coordinates on screen.
Save and organize project workspace files.
w20.controlOfError: Event trigger response. Clicking the trigger reliably resets and starts sprite positions.

w21.activityName: Applied Capstone Phase 2: Logic, Loops & Variables
w21.bigIdea: Core application behavior relies on dynamic state variables (scores, timers) governed by continuous loops and conditional checks.
w21.setupPrep: Prepare code snippet reference cards for score incrementing, loop execution, and collision detection ('if touching sprite').
w21.title: Applied Capstone Phase 2: Digital Logic Implementation
w21.primaryDesc: Add repeat loops and motion blocks in ScratchJr to automate sprite animations.
w21.elementaryDesc: Program conditional logic loops (if/else) and state variables (moisture_level, score) in Scratch.
steps: Implement motion logic and directional key controls.
Create a Score variable to keep track of points.
Add IF/THEN condition blocks for sprite collisions (e.g., IF touching target THEN change score by 1).
Implement repeating loops for continuous background motion or timer countdowns.
Test individual code scripts sequentially.
w21.controlOfError: Variable update verification. Score correctly increments upon collision event.

w22.activityName: Applied Capstone Phase 3: Systematic Peer Testing & Debugging
w22.bigIdea: Software quality assurance requires systematic peer testing, probing edge cases, logging unexpected glitches, and refactoring code.
w22.setupPrep: Print Peer Bug Report logs. Establish quiet peer-review pairs with clear testing protocols (e.g., 5 min testing, 5 min logging).
w22.title: Applied Capstone Phase 3: Testing & Debugging
w22.primaryDesc: Peer test ScratchJr projects; spot missing block links when sprite fails to move.
w22.elementaryDesc: Conduct systematic peer testing, log edge cases, and debug variable state glitches or path collisions.
steps: Pair students up to conduct peer playtesting of each other's capstone projects.
Testers attempt edge cases (e.g., pressing wrong buttons, running into boundaries).
Record discovered bugs or unexpected behavior on a Debugging Log.
Programmers isolate and fix identified bugs in their project code.
Refactor long scripts into cleaner loops or subroutines.
w22.controlOfError: Successful peer re-testing confirming bug resolution.

w23.bigIdea: User experience (UX) design and clear verbal presentation are crucial for communicating technological solutions to an audience.
w23.setupPrep: Print Display Card templates for student project stands. Set up presentation stations around the perimeter of the room.
w23.title: Project Polishing & Presentation Prep
w23.primaryDesc: Practice explaining ScratchJr app controls to teacher; polish sprite visuals.
w23.elementaryDesc: Refine user interface aesthetics, write project documentation, and create showcase presentation cards.
steps: Add finishing touches: title screen, instruction text, sound effects, and game over screen.
Create physical display cards explaining the CS Unplugged concept behind their project.
Practice presenting projects verbally to small groups.
Give constructive feedback on peer delivery and clarity.
Finalize project setups for showcase day.
w23.controlOfError: Presentation checklist complete with title screen, clear rules, and working demo.

w24.activityName: Year-End CS Living Museum & Community Showcase
w24.bigIdea: Sharing computational artifacts with a broader community validates learning, fosters mentorship, and celebrates creative achievement.
w24.setupPrep: Transform classroom into museum stations (Unplugged grids, Parity magic trick table, Sorting network, Digital Capstone stations). Print Certificates.
keyMaterials: Unplugged activity props (grids, cards, cipher wheels)
w24.title: Year-End CS Living Museum & Community Showcase
w24.primaryDesc: Demonstrate Kidbot floor grid mazes and ScratchJr apps to parents and community guests.
w24.elementaryDesc: Exhibit Capstone digital tools (Eco-Sorter / Garden Tracker) and guide visitors through unplugged stations.
steps: Set up classroom stations representing key activities across Trimesters 1, 2, and 3.
Welcome parents, teachers, and visitors to the Living CS Museum.
Students guide visitors through live unplugged challenges (e.g., Jam Sandwich Robot, Parity Magic trick, Sorting Network).
Demonstrate completed capstone digital projects.
Celebrate student achievement with CS Unplugged completion certificates!
w24.controlOfError: Successful visitor participation and student-led activity completion.

lab.activityName: Open Lab: Ozobot Hardware Integration & Digital Portfolios
lab.bigIdea: Bridging unplugged algorithms to physical robotics (Ozobots) and compiling digital portfolios solidifies long-term computational mastery.
lab.setupPrep: Charge Ozobot robots. Distribute color-code markers (Red, Blue, Green, Black) and butcher paper tracks. Set up digital portfolio folders.
lab.title: Open Lab / Buffer: Extension, Hardware Bridge & Portfolio Completion
lab.primaryDesc: Ozobot line-following code markers and open exploration on floor tracks.
lab.elementaryDesc: Ozobot integration, open Scratch coding exploration, and digital portfolio compilation.
steps: Demonstrate Ozobot line-following markers (color codes for speed, turns, and loops).
Have Primary students construct custom paper mazes for Ozobots to navigate.
Have Elementary students program Ozobots using Ozoblockly or continue open Scratch exploration.
Compile student work samples, photographs, and code reflection sheets into individual portfolios.
Host a final classroom celebration and wrap-up.
lab.controlOfError: Robot color code reading. Ozobot flashes colored LED and executes command upon reading code marker.
